I farm on the North China Plain, so I will keep to the system I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In Quzhou County, that rotation fits my land, water, labor, and weather better than trying to chase riskier cash crops. I do not have formal schooling, so I will stick with a simple plan I know how to manage well and can carry through on time. Wheat gives me a steady grain harvest, and maize after wheat makes full use of the same land for the whole year.

For wheat, I will manage it as my main winter crop and push for a stable yield instead of gambling on very high input use. I will use improved seed, apply enough nitrogen for strong tillering and grain filling, add phosphorus for roots, and some potassium to support the stand. I will irrigate several times because spring here can turn dry, and I will spray only when disease, aphids, or weeds justify it. I will use rotary tillage for the wheat side because it is practical and common for me.

After wheat harvest, I will plant summer maize quickly so I do not lose soil moisture or growing time. I will use hybrid maize because the yield is better and more dependable for me. I will give maize the heavier nitrogen feeding, with moderate phosphorus and potassium, and I will irrigate fewer times than wheat unless the season turns dry. I will keep pesticide sprays limited and timely, mainly for weeds and major insect pressure. This way I use my land fully, keep the work straightforward, and aim for dependable grain production across the whole year.
